claim: Cells use signal relay to transmit information across tissue scales.
source: Cells use signal relay to transmit information across tissue scales.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the subsequent experimental findings and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Migration is triggered by an increase in wave frequency generated at the signalling centre.
source: Combining imaging and optogenetic perturbation of cell signalling states, we find that migration is triggered by an increase in wave frequency generated at the signalling centre.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data combining imaging and optogenetic perturbation as stated in the abstract.

claim: Wave frequency is regulated by cAMP wave circulation.
source: Wave frequency is regulated by cAMP wave circulation, which organises the long-range signal.
evidence: This is a finding from the study as stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations.

claim: Models in which cell density and spatial patterning modulate the wave frequency cannot explain the temporal evolution of signalling waves.
source: Models in which cell density and spatial patterning modulate the wave frequency cannot explain the temporal evolution of signalling waves.
evidence: This is a conclusion from testing competing models as described in the abstract.

claim: Wave circulation increases the ability for cells to relay the signal, causing further increase in the circulation rate.
source: Instead, our evidence leads to a model where wave circulation increases the ability for cells to relay the signal, causing further increase in the circulation rate.
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the evidence presented in the study.

claim: Positive feedback between cell state and signalling pattern regulates the long-range signal coding that drives morphogenesis.
source: This positive feedback between cell state and signalling pattern regulates the long-range signal coding that drives morphogenesis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: Signal diffusion is only efficient over a few cell diameters.
source: As signal diffusion is only efficient over a few cell diameters, cells relay signals to rapidly disseminate information over tissue scales (Gelens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gelens et al., 2014.

claim: Signals are relayed by the activation of cells in response to active neighbours, which in turn activate their own neighbours.
source: Signals are relayed by the activation of cells in response to active neighbours, which in turn activate their own neighbours (Dieterle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dieterle et al., 2020.

claim: Long-range signalling through tissues is propagated as waves of cell activation that travel outwardly from signalling centres.
source: In this way, long-range signalling through tissues is propagated as waves of cell activation that travel outwardly from signalling centres (Deneke and Di Talia, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Deneke and Di Talia, 2018.

claim: ERK waves occur in the developing skin, breast, and colon and during wound closure.
source: Prominent examples of biological activation waves include ERK waves in the developing skin, breast, and colon and during wound closure (Aoki et al., 2017; Ender et al., 2022; Pond et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aoki et al., 2017; Ender et al., 2022; Pond et al., 2022.

claim: Periodic activation waves occur in the brain.
source: periodic activation waves in the brain (Huang et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2010.

claim: Chemoattractant waves occur in neutrophil swarms.
source: chemoattractant waves in neutrophil swarms (Afonso et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Afonso et al., 2012.

claim: Morphogen waves occur during gastrulation.
source: morphogen waves during gastrulation (Liu et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: Waves of cell stress occur in bacterial biofilms.
source: waves of cell stress in bacterial biofilms (Chou et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chou et al., 2022.

claim: cAMP waves occur in Dictyostelium aggregation.
source: cAMP waves in Dictyostelium aggregation (Tomchik and Devreotes, 1981)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tomchik and Devreotes, 1981.

claim: Waves can be pathological, such as in cardiac fibrillation, where waves drive muscle contraction independently of the pacemaker.
source: Waves can also be pathological, such as in cardiac fibrillation, where waves drive muscle contraction independently of the pacemaker (Pandit and Jalife, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pandit and Jalife, 2013.

claim: Upon starvation, single Dictyostelium cells begin to communicate via cAMP.
source: Upon starvation, single cells begin to communicate via cAMP (Tomchik and Devreotes, 1981; Gregor et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tomchik and Devreotes, 1981; Gregor et al., 2010.

claim: Upon receipt of cAMP, cells secrete their own cAMP, which then activates the next set of cells, hence propagating the signal.
source: Upon receipt of cAMP, cells secrete their own cAMP, which then activates the next set of cells, hence propagating the signal.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Dictyostelium signaling.

claim: cAMP is a chemoattractant.
source: As cAMP is a chemoattractant, cells move towards signalling centres, resulting in aggregation into the multicellular phase of their lifecycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cAMP function in Dictyostelium.

claim: The cAMP signal propagates in waves with circular and spiral patterns characteristic of other relay systems.
source: At the population level, the cAMP signal propagates in waves with circular and spiral patterns characteristic of other relay systems (Durston, 1973; Lee et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Durston, 1973; Lee et al., 1996.

claim: Information is carried by cAMP wave gradient, frequency, and speed and decoded by cells in terms of changes in motility.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest information is carried by cAMP wave gradient, frequency, and speed and decoded by cells in terms of changes in motility (Siegert and Weijer, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siegert and Weijer, 1989.

claim: Cells interpret an increase in the frequency of the cAMP waves as a trigger to begin collective chemotaxis.
source: One view is that cells interpret an increase in the frequency of the cAMP waves as a trigger to begin collective chemotaxis (Skoge et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Skoge et al., 2014.

claim: Other changing features of the waves, such as their speed and gradient, convey information instructing chemotaxis.
source: Alternative views are that other changing features of the waves, such as their speed and gradient, convey information instructing chemotaxis (Fisher et al., 1989; Wessels et al., 1992; Song et al., 2006; Nakajima et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fisher et al., 1989; Wessels et al., 1992; Song et al., 2006; Nakajima et al., 2014.

claim: The excitability of cell groups increases at higher cell densities, which then manifests in the changing wave dynamics coupled to the onset of aggregation.
source: The current paradigm explaining the changes in wave behaviour over developmental time is that the excitability (the ability to relay the signal) of cell groups increases (individual cell excitability remains constant) at higher cell densities, which then manifests in the changing wave dynamics coupled to the onset of aggregation (Höfer et al., 1995; van Oss et al., 1996; Dallon and Othmer, 1997).
evidence: This is the current paradigm supported by citations to Höfer et al., 1995; van Oss et al., 1996; Dallon and Othmer, 1997.

claim: The curvature and rotation rate of spiral waves are specified by the circulation of the signal at the signalling centre.
source: The curvature and rotation rate are specified by the circulation of the signal at the signalling centre (Tyson and Keener, 1988; Winfree, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tyson and Keener, 1988; Winfree, 2001.

claim: Dictyostelium AX3 cells were engineered to express Flamindo2 and H2B-mCherry from safe-haven genomic locations for stable and uniform expression.
source: Dictyostelium AX3 cells were engineered to express Flamindo2 and H2B-mCherry from safe-haven genomic locations for stable and uniform expression.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Flamindo2 is a cAMP biosensor with a fluorescence intensity that is inversely proportional to internal cAMP levels.
source: Flamindo2 is a cAMP biosensor (Odaka et al., 2014; Hashimura et al., 2019) with a fluorescence intensity that is inversely proportional to internal cAMP levels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Odaka et al., 2014; Hashimura et al., 2019.

claim: A codon-optimised sequence encoding the Flamindo2 reporter was knocked-in to the act5 locus for stable and uniform expression.
source: A codon-optimised sequence encoding the Flamindo2 reporter was knocked-in to the act5 locus for stable and uniform expression (Paschke et al., 2018; Tunnacliffe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods supported by citations to Paschke et al., 2018; Tunnacliffe et al., 2018.

claim: H2B-mCherry, knocked into the rps30 locus, labels the nucleus for cell tracking at high cell densities.
source: H2B-mCherry, knocked into the rps30 locus, labels the nucleus for cell tracking at highcell densities (Corrigan and Chubb, 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods supported by a citation to Corrigan and Chubb, 2014.

claim: Early during development, cells predominantly fired asynchronously.
source: Early during development, cells predominantly fired asynchronously.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The proportion of spontaneously activating cells declined as the signalling behaviour became more correlated, with periodic waves of signalling including an increasing proportion of the cells.
source: The proportion of spontaneously activating cells declined as the signalling behaviour became more correlated, with periodic waves of signalling including an increasing proportion of the cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: During early development, the population distribution of inter-activation intervals follows a gamma distribution.
source: During this time, the population distribution of inter-activation intervals follows a gamma distribution (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The initial cAMP waves (around 4–5 hr) are broad bands of broken waves amalgamating from numerous circular patterns that expand from spontaneously activating cells.
source: The initial cAMP waves (around 4–5 hr) are broad bands of broken waves amalgamating from numerous circular patterns that expand from spontaneously activating cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Rotating spiral cAMP waves form from broken waves around 5–6 hr following starvation.
source: Rotating spiral cAMP waves form from broken waves around 5–6 hr following starvation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Wave breaks occurred only when the oncoming wave collided with an asymmetric wave generated by the activated patch.
source: Wave breaks (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A forth – sixth row) occurred only when the oncoming wave collided with an asymmetric wave generated by the activated patch (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A third row).
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Rotating spiral patterns generate waves that are more frequent and regular than circular patterns.
source: Rotating spiral patterns generate waves that are more frequent and regular than circular patterns (Figure 1 5-6 hr onwards) and hence become the dominant pattern over time, overriding the less frequent circular waves, as reported in previous studies (Lee et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data and supported by a citation to Lee et al., 1996.

claim: The mean wave frequency steadily increased towards the maximum firing frequency of cells, around once every 3–4 min.
source: The mean wave frequency steadily increased towards the maximum firing frequency of cells, around once every 3–4 min (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The proportion of spontaneously activating cells tends to zero as there is no time to activate between waves.
source: Consequently, the proportion of spontaneously activating cells tends to zero as there is no time to activate between waves (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The population distribution of inter-pulse intervals tends to a normal distribution as wave frequency increases.
source: and the population distribution of inter-pulse intervals tends to a normal distribution (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A cell that fires ahead of its neighbours has a 60% chance of repeating this early firing, 35% chance of switching to late firing, and a 5% chance of skipping the subsequent wave.
source: Aided by Markov modelling, we observed a short-term bias in firing tendencies: for example, a cell that fires ahead of its neighbours has a 60% chance of repeating this early firing, 35% chance of switching to late firing, and a 5% chance of skipping the subsequent wave (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data and Markov modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, D.

claim: The spatial organisation and motility of cells changed rapidly, occurring around 7 hr following starvation, coincident with the dominance of spiral waves.
source: The spatial organisation and motility of cells changed rapidly, occurring around 7 hr following starvation, coincident with the dominance of spiral waves (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: During the transition to collective migration, cAMP waves steadily became more frequent, slower and thinner, and cells became faster, more directional, and persistent in their movement.
source: During this process, cAMP waves steadily became more frequent, slower and thinner, and cells became faster, more directional, and persistent in their movement (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The profile of the mean cAMP pulse in single cells remained constant with each wave.
source: The profile of the mean cAMP pulse in single cells remained constant with each wave.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: A thinner wave generates a steeper external cAMP gradient, which may enhance chemotaxis.
source: A thinner wave generates a steeper external cAMP gradient, which may enhance chemotaxis (Song et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Song et al., 2006.

claim: Cells consistently moved towards the wave source at wave fronts but remained spatially uniform before 6 hr of starvation due to random cell motion at the wave rear.
source: Cells consistently moved towards the wave source at wave fronts but remained spatially uniform before 6 hr of starvation due to random cell motion at the wave rear (Figure 2B bottom left panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: For infrequent, fast and wide waves (i.e. circular patterns), the chemotaxis index and local correlation of cell motion reached their baseline values at the following wave front, indicating cells move randomly.
source: For infrequent, fast and wide waves (i.e. circular patterns), the chemotaxis index and local correlation of cell motion reached their baseline values at the following wave front, indicating cells move randomly.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: From 6.5 hr onwards, when the wave period is less than 4.5 min, the measures of collective cell motion do not relax back to their previous values by the next wave and hence gradually increase over time to constant, elevated values across the entire wave.
source: From 6.5 hr onwards, when the wave period is less than 4.5 min, the measures of collective cell motion do not relax back to their previous values by the next wave and hence gradually increase over time to constant, elevated values across the entire wave (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The cell speed at the front of the wave increases incrementally with each wave until it peaks at around 7 µm min−1.
source: In parallel, the cell speed at the front of the wave increases incrementally with each wave until it peaks at around 7 µm min−1 (Figure 2D second panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cells collectively migrated towards the signalling centre only when the induced wave period was less than 4.5 min.
source: Consistent with our observations shown in Figure 2, cells collectively migrated towards the signalling centre only when the induced wave period was less than 4.5 min (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Photoactivation of cells with a period less than 3.5 min did not result in aggregation.
source: However, photoactivation of cells with a period less than 3.5 min did not result in aggregation.
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Cells cannot relay a steady periodic signal close to their maximum firing rate initially, resulting in a missed wave every second photoactivation event.
source: We infer that this is because cells cannot relay a steady periodic signal close to their maximum firing rate initially, resulting in a missed wave every second photoactivation event (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is an inference from the optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Photoactivating cells at a gradually increasing frequency from 5 min to 3.5 min intervals resulted in the accumulation of a significantly larger number of cells around the signalling centre and conglomerates of several aggregates.
source: Motivated by the observed change in wave frequency during aggregation, we sought to test if it were possible to induce large cell aggregates by photoactivating cells at a faster rate than what we observe experimentally by reducing the wave period gradually from 5 min to 3.5 min from 5 to 6 hr following starvation, rather than 6–8 hr (Figure 3C second panel). This was indeed achievable, resulting in the accumulation of a significantly larger number of cells around the signalling centre and conglomerates of several aggregates (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The spiral tip will sustain itself and the entire spiral wave by virtue of circular motion.
source: Based on the general theory of excitable media, the spiral tip will sustain itself and the entire spiral wave by virtue of circular motion (Tyson and Keener, 1988; Winfree, 2001).
evidence: This is based on the general theory of excitable media supported by citations to Tyson and Keener, 1988; Winfree, 2001.

claim: The circulation of the spiral tip is the organising source of the spiral wave.
source: In other words, the circulation of the spiral tip is the organising source of the spiral wave.
evidence: This is based on the general theory of excitable media.

claim: Spiral waves significantly change in rotation rate and curvature during aggregation.
source: Spiral waves significantly change in rotation rate and curvature during aggregation, which we refer to as spiral wave progression (Figure 4C and Figure 4—videos 1–3).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—videos 1–3.

claim: Each rotation of the spiral tip generates a wave: the rate at which the activation waves circulate around the signalling centre sets the frequency of global activation waves disseminated from the signalling centre.
source: Each rotation of the spiral tip generates a wave: the rate at which the activation waves circulate around the signalling centre sets the frequency of global activation waves disseminated from the signalling centre.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The spiral tip rotational period decreased from 5.5 min to 3.5 min.
source: The spiral tip rotational period decreased from 5.5 min to 3.5 min.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The radius of circulation steadily reduced from around 100 µm to 20 µm during spiral wave progression.
source: The acceleration of spiral tip circulation is associated with spiral core contraction; the radius of circulation steadily reduced from around 100 µm to 20 µm (Figure 4D second panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: During spiral core contraction, the spiral tip speed decreased from 100 to 120 to 40–50 µm min−1.
source: Meanwhile, during this contraction, the spiral tip speed decreased from 100 to 120 to 40–50 µm min−1 (Figure 4D third panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The activation parameter and planar wave speed both decrease during spiral wave progression.
source: This analysis reveals that the activation parameter and planar wave speed both decrease during spiral wave progression (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The planar wave speed halves in value as the wave period decreases towards its minimum.
source: Firstly, we find that the planar wave speed halves in value as the wave period decreases towards its minimum (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: As the wave period decreases, cells have less time to reset between waves, causing slower cell activation and wave speed (the dispersion relation).
source: The theory of excitable media provides the following interpretation: as the wave period decreases, cells have less time to reset between waves, causing slower cell activation and wave speed (the dispersion relation)
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the theory of excitable media.

claim: The circulation of the spiral tip determines the wave speed away from the core, in addition to the frequency.
source: This deceleration quantitatively matches the changing wave dynamics away from the spiral core (Figures 2C and 5B), meaning the circulation of the spiral tip determines the wave speed away from the core, in addition to the frequency.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 5B.

claim: The increase in spiral wave rotation rate and curvature is a consequence of cells becoming more excitable over time.
source: Secondly, the theory interprets the increase in spiral wave rotation rate and curvature to be a consequence of cells becoming more excitable over time (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the theory of excitable media and experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The activation parameter collapses onto a highly consistent curve when plotted against the wave period.
source: Indeed, although there was temporal variation between experimental replicates, the activation parameter collapses onto a highly consistent curve when plotted against the wave period (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A substantial decrease in the cell activation parameter and increase in cell density occur during spiral wave progression.
source: Consistent with this paradigm, we measured a substantial decrease in the cell activation parameter (inverse of cell excitability) and increase in cell density during spiral wave progression (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The relationship between density and the activation parameter is incredibly sensitive, meaning slight fluctuations in density would correspond to dramatic changes in the activation parameter.
source: The relationship between density and the activation parameter is incredibly sensitive, meaning slight fluctuations in density (such as occurring through random motility) would correspond to dramatic changes in the activation parameter (Figure 6C first panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A causative relationship between density and excitability is not supported by reliable fits.
source: However, unlike the strong relationship between wave period and cell excitability (Figures 5C and 6C third panel), a causative relationship between density and excitability is not supported by reliable fits (Figure 6C second panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Spiral wave progression occurs prior to clear changes in cell density.
source: In addition, our data show that spiral wave progression occurs prior to clear changes in cell density (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Spiral core contraction and the increase in rotation rate are immediate and steady for around 1.5 hr following spiral wave formation.
source: Specifically, spiral core contraction and the increase in rotation rate are immediate and steady for around 1.5 hr following spiral wave formation (Figure 6B second panel)
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The cell density sharply increases only after around 1 hr once the wave period is below 4.5 min.
source: while the cell density sharply increases only after around 1 hr (Figure 6B first panel) once the wave period is below 4.5 min.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The rotational period is close to the minimum value before substantial changes in density occur.
source: Indeed, the rotational period is close to the minimum value before substantial changes in density occur (Figure 6B third panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: An increase in cell density is not sufficient to account for spiral wave progression, at least at the onset of collective migration.
source: Altogether, these observations imply that an increase in cell density is not sufficient to account for spiral wave progression, at least at the onset of collective migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of experimental data.

claim: The hybrid PDE agent-based model reproduced a rotating spiral wave and experimentally observed spatial patterning of cells.
source: This model reproduced a rotating spiral wave and experimentally observed spatial patterning of cells (Figure 7, Figure 7—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The rotating spiral wave creates a limit cycle in cell motion.
source: In the model, the rotating spiral wave creates a limit cycle in cell motion (see the circular streamline in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results and experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells collect along the limit cycle via chemotaxis from both inside and outside the path of tip circulation, forming a ring pattern.
source: Cells collect along the limit cycle via chemotaxis from both inside and outside the path of tip circulation, forming a ring pattern.
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results and experimental data.

claim: In data and model, both the radius of spiral tip circulation and the ring pattern of cells contract over time.
source: In data and model, both the radius of spiral tip circulation and the ring pattern of cells contract over time.
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results and experimental data.

claim: Spiral core contraction occurred in the absence of cell-cell physical interactions but not in the absence of cell motion.
source: In our model, this contraction occurred in the absence of cell-cell physical interactions (i.e. no crowding effects) but not in the absence of cell motion (Figure 7D and E first panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: Spiral core contraction can be attributed to the spatial reorganisation of cells via chemotaxis towards the circulating wave, but not necessarily due to crowding effects from cells funnelling towards the spiral core.
source: These tests indicate that spiral core contraction can be attributed to the spatial reorganisation of cells via chemotaxis towards the circulating wave, but not necessarily due to crowding effects from cells funnelling towards the spiral core.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: The spiral wave does not increase in rotation rate during spiral core contraction in the model with constant cell excitability.
source: Specifically, the spiral wave does not increase in rotation rate during spiral core contraction (Figure 7E second and third panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The speed of spiral tip motion decreases too much to offset the contraction in the radius of circulation in the model with constant cell excitability.
source: The speed of spiral tip motion decreases too much to offset the contraction in the radius of circulation (Figure 7E fourth panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results shown in Figure 7E.

claim: By adding an additional component to the model, which allows the excitability of individual cells to increase over time, the model outputs a strong increase in wave frequency.
source: By adding an additional component to the model, which allows the excitability of individual cells to increase over time, this flaw can be bypassed, with the model outputting a strong increase in wave frequency (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—video 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—video 3.

claim: Cell state is similar across the field during spiral wave progression.
source: Due to the conservation of the rotational period at the signalling centre and wave period away from the signalling centre, one consequence of Hypothesis 2 is that cell state should be similar across the field.
evidence: This is a prediction from Hypothesis 2.

claim: There is a consistent dispersion relation both at and away from the spiral core.
source: Using this approach, we find a consistent dispersion relation both at and away from the spiral core (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The changes in cell state due to wave dynamics are the same across the population.
source: In other words, the changes in cell state due to wave dynamics are the same across the population.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of experimental data.

claim: The adapted Tyson model reproduces features of spiral wave progression such as the rate of spiral core contraction, increase in spiral wave curvature, increase in the spiral rotation rate, and the coupling between the cell activation parameter and the wave period.
source: This solution reproduces features of spiral wave progression such as the rate of spiral core contraction (Figure 8B), increase in spiral wave curvature, increase in the spiral rotation rate, and the coupling between the cell activation parameter and the wave period (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: The positive feedback between cell excitability and the wave period is a sufficient mechanism driving spiral wave progression.
source: The similarity between our experimental data and this model (even with parameter values rounded to the nearest order of magnitude) suggests that the positive feedback between cell excitability and the wave period is a sufficient mechanism driving spiral wave progression (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The change in predicted radius precedes the change in the measured radius, with convergence at the end of spiral wave progression.
source: Further supporting Hypothesis 2, our data show the change in predicted radius precedes the change in the measured radius, with convergence at the end of spiral wave progression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The radius of spiral tip circulation is a consequence, not driver, of spiral wave progression.
source: That is, the radius of spiral tip circulation is a consequence, not driver, of spiral wave progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of experimental data.

claim: The inclusion of a hole in the cell density field does not hinder spiral wave progression in the adapted Tyson model.
source: Exploring the properties of the radius contraction in the adapted Tyson model shows that the inclusion of a hole in the cell density field does not hinder spiral wave progression.
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results.

claim: The spiral wave becomes pinned to the hole, which sets the minimum radius of spiral tip circulation.
source: The spiral wave becomes pinned to the hole, which sets the minimum radius of spiral tip circulation (Figure 8B and Figure 8—video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—video 2.

claim: The wave period reduces because the speed of the spiral tip speed remains elevated by virtue of an increase in excitability, compensating for a large radius of circulation.
source: The wave period reduces (Figure 8C third panel) because the speed of the spiral tip speed remains elevated (Figure 8C second panel) by virtue of an increase in excitability (Figure 8C fourth and fifth panel), compensating for a large radius of circulation (Figure 8C first panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Spiral waves can become pinned to physical blocks.
source: Spiral waves can become pinned to the blocks (Figure 9A), with their minimum radius of circulation set by the block radius (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments with physical blocks shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: Spiral waves that are pinned to a block cannot fully contract but nevertheless undergo a steady increase in rotation rate and hence decrease in wave rotational period.
source: Spiral waves that are pinned to a block cannot fully contract (Figure 9C first panel) but nevertheless undergo a steady increase in rotation rate and hence decrease in wave rotational period (Figure 9C third panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments with physical blocks shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The circulation rate increases because the spiral tip speed does not decrease to the same extent as the unconstrained spirals.
source: The circulation rate increases because the spiral tip speed does not decrease to the same extent as the unconstrained spirals (Figure 9C second panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments with physical blocks shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The contraction of the spiral tip circulation is a consequence, not a driver, of spiral wave progression.
source: Together, these observations are consistent with Hypothesis 2, but not Hypothesis 1: the contraction of the spiral tip circulation is a consequence, not a driver, of spiral wave progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments with physical blocks.

claim: Spiral wave progression results from positive feedback between cell excitability and wave frequency, arising only in the context of the spiral wave pattern.
source: Overall, our approach provides a clear interpretation of our data that spiral wave progression results from positive feedback between cell excitability and wave frequency, arising only in the context of the spiral wave pattern (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The activation waves are organised as a multi-armed spiral in aggregates.
source: Previous studies show the activation waves are organised as a multi-armed spiral in aggregates (Siegert and Weijer, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siegert and Weijer, 1995.

claim: Single-armed spirals destabilise only once the cellular ring fully contracts.
source: Single-armed spirals destabilise only once the cellular ring fully contracts.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Contraction results in a phase singularity that is fixed at the aggregate centre.
source: Contraction results in a phase singularity (convergence of all signalling phases) that is fixed at the aggregate centre (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The phase singularity and spiral wave are unstable and disintegrate over time.
source: The phase singularity and spiral wave are unstable and disintegrate over time.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The cells at the centre cannot activate at a rate necessary to support the full spectrum of signalling phases.
source: This is likely because the cells are not infinitely small and can only be in one signalling phase at a time. In other words, the cells at the centre cannot activate at a rate necessary to support the full spectrum of signalling phases.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The destabilisation process begins by cells signalling out-of-phase with the spiral wave, resulting in the emergence of transient patches of cell activation that gradually increase in number, size, and lifetime.
source: The destabilisation process begins by cells signalling out-of-phase with the spiral wave, resulting in the emergence of transient patches of cell activation that gradually increase in number, size, and lifetime (Figure 10, around 2 hr following spiral formation).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The single-armed spiral has a rotational period of 3.4±0.2 min, which is three times faster than the three-armed spiral whose rotational period is 10.1±0.7 min and wave period is 3.3±0.5 min.
source: These data show that the single-armed spiral (<2 hr) has a rotational period of 3.4±0.2 min (the minimum cell firing period, see Figures 1, 3 and 4), which is three times faster than the three-armed spiral whose rotational period is 10.1±0.7 min and wave period is 3.3±0.5 min.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of experimental data.

claim: The overall frequency with which a cell experiences a wave is the same for both single-armed and three-armed spirals.
source: This means that the overall frequency with which a cell experiences a wave is the same because the three-armed spiral provides three waves in its longer rotation period.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Both single-armed and multi-armed spiral patterns encode the same temporal information.
source: As such, the frequency of cAMP waves disseminated from the signalling centre, along the streams, remains the same for both signalling patterns. That is, both patterns encode the same temporal information.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of experimental data.

claim: The signalling pattern adapts to the change in aggregate geometry while maintaining an active phase wave that generates waves at the maximum frequency.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that the signalling pattern adapts to the change in aggregate geometry while maintaining an active phase wave that generates waves at the maximum frequency.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of experimental data.

claim: Cell aggregation is coordinated by the dynamics of circulating waves of cell activation at the signalling centre.
source: Our analysis shows how cell aggregation is coordinated by the dynamics of circulating waves of cell activation at the signalling centre.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The circulation rate modulates the speed, frequency, and width of long-range periodic activation waves, spatially organised as a spiral.
source: The circulation rate modulates the speed, frequency, and width of long-range periodic activation waves, spatially organised as a spiral.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The increase in the circulation rate arises due to positive feedback between the cell signalling pattern and cell signalling state.
source: Using the general theory of excitable media, mathematical modelling, and physical perturbations of population structure, our data imply the increase in the circulation rate arises due to positive feedback between the cell signalling pattern and cell signalling state.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The wave circulation rate is determined by the ability of cells to relay the signal (cell excitability), whilst the ability to relay increases as the circulation rate increases.
source: Specifically, the wave circulation rate is determined by the ability of cells to relay the signal (cell excitability), whilst the ability to relay increases as the circulation rate increases.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The information encoding a morphogenetic transition unfolds from positive feedback between the signalling pattern and the cell signalling properties at the signalling centre.
source: As such, the information encoding a morphogenetic transition unfolds from positive feedback between the signalling pattern and the cell signalling properties at the signalling centre.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The collective behaviour of 10^5–10^6 cells across several millimetres is organised by circulation of a self-sustaining signal over 10^2–10^3 cells.
source: Altogether, our results describe how the collective behaviour of 105–106 cells across several millimetres is organised by circulation of a self-sustaining signal over 102–103 cells.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Biological activation waves can encode information that can be modulated and translated to changes in the spatial organisation and gene expression of individuals beyond the spatial scale of the individual, which can feedback to changes in activation wave dynamics and structure.
source: The difference is that biological activation waves can encode information that can be modulated and translated to changes in the spatial organisation and gene expression of individuals beyond the spatial scale of the individual, which can feedback to changes in activation wave dynamics and structure.
evidence: This is a general conclusion from the study.

claim: For Dictyostelium aggregation, information is generated locally by the rate of circulation of the spiral tip and decoded globally by cell chemotaxis.
source: For Dictyostelium aggregation, information is generated locally by the rate of circulation of the spiral tip and decoded globally by cell chemotaxis.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The ability for cells to move collectively increases with an increase in wave frequency.
source: One view is that the ability for cells to move collectively increases with an increase in wave frequency. Skoge et al., 2014 showed, by controlling the frequency of cAMP waves, that the chemotactic index increased as the frequency became maximal (Skoge et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Skoge et al., 2014.

claim: Artificial rotating waves revealed that 4–5 waves at high frequency can induce cell polarity migration.
source: An alternative view is that cells 'count' waves: artificial rotating waves revealed that 4–5 waves at high frequency can induce cell polarity migration (Nakajima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nakajima et al., 2016.

claim: Cells move maximally towards steep stationary and/or increasing gradients over time.
source: An alternative view is based on the wave gradient, where cells move maximally towards steep stationary (Fisher et al., 1989; Song et al., 2006) and/or increasing (Varnum et al., 1985; Wessels et al., 1992; Nakajima et al., 2014) gradients over time.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fisher et al., 1989; Song et al., 2006; Varnum et al., 1985; Wessels et al., 1992; Nakajima et al., 2014.

claim: All the wave properties: speed, frequency, and width are specified by the circulation of the spiral tip.
source: What our study shows is that all the wave properties: speed, frequency, and width are specified by the circulation of the spiral tip.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Once the frequency is set by the tip, all other features are set by default.
source: Specifically, once the frequency is set by the tip, all other features are set by default.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The circulation rate of the signal at the signalling centre is the mechanism of information production, regardless of the specific information-decoding mechanism.
source: Altogether, our study implies that the circulation rate of the signal at the signalling centre is the mechanism of information production, regardless of the specific information-decoding mechanism.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Expression of pdsA, which encodes a cAMP phosphodiaterase, and csaA, which encodes a cell-cell adhesion protein, is sensitive to the changing frequency of cAMP pulses.
source: Expression of pdsA, which encodes a cAMP phosphodiaterase, and csaA, which encodes a cell-cell adhesion protein, is sensitive to the changing frequency of cAMP pulses (Masaki et al., 2013; Corrigan and Chubb, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Masaki et al., 2013; Corrigan and Chubb, 2014.

claim: The csaA gene is induced during infrequent cAMP signalling, then inactivated as the pulse frequency increases as cells aggregate.
source: The csaA gene is induced during infrequent cAMP signalling, then inactivated as the pulse frequency increases as cells aggregate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about csaA gene regulation.

claim: The transcription factor GataC displays rapid shuttling between the nucleus and cytoplasm in response to external cAMP oscillations.
source: The transcription factor GataC displays rapid shuttling between the nucleus and cytoplasm in response to external cAMP oscillations (Cai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cai et al., 2014.

claim: GataC nucleocytoplasmic shuttling is low-pass filtered, occurring only when external cAMP oscillations reach a threshold frequency.
source: This process is low-pass filtered, with nucleocytoplasmic shuttling occurring only when external cAMP oscillations reach a threshold frequency.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GataC regulation.

claim: The temporal coding of cAMP waves allows cells to sense the extent of cell aggregation through the frequency of activation waves produced by the aggregate, which increases as aggregation progresses.
source: In Dictyostelium, the temporal coding of cAMP waves allows cells to sense the extent of cell aggregation through the frequency of activation waves produced by the aggregate, which increases as aggregation progresses.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.

claim: The temporal code allows for long-range sensing of aggregate progression, which can be interpreted as a non-local quorum sensing mechanism.
source: In other words, the temporal code allows for long-range sensing of aggregate progression, which can be interpreted as a non-local quorum sensing mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.

claim: By moving only towards highly frequent and consistent cAMP waves, effort is concentrated on migration directed only towards an established signalling centre.
source: A potential advantage of this adaptive information coding system is that by moving only towards highly frequent and consistent cAMP waves, effort is then concentrated on migration directed only towards an established signalling centre.
evidence: This is a speculation about the advantage of the system.

claim: The transition to the multi-armed spiral is an adaption to the change in aggregate geometry to maintain an active phase wave at the signalling centre that generates activation waves at the maximum frequency.
source: Overall, we view the transition to the multi-armed spiral as an adaption to the change in aggregate geometry to maintain an active phase wave at the signalling centre that generates activation waves at the maximum frequency.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.
